etymologies.etymologyHTML: From circa 1305, Middle English podynge (“kind of sausage; meat-filled animal stomach”), puddynge, from Old French boudin (“blood sausage, black pudding”), from Latin botellus (“sausage, small intestine”). Doublet of boudin.

definitions.definition: Any of various dishes, sweet or savoury, prepared by boiling or steaming, or from batter.

quote.citation: 2004, Victoria Wise, The Pressure Cooker Gourmet, page 313:
quote.text: The dishes in this chapter represent a range of multiethnic savory custards and steamed puddings, including a few surprises like a chèvre popover pudding and a bread pudding with lettuce and cheese.

quote.citation: 2004, Sarah Garland, The Complete Book of Herbs & Spices, page 199:
quote.text: Steamed and boiled puddings have formed the basic diet of country people in northern Europe for centuries. Early puddings consisted of the scoured stomach of a sheep or pig, stuffed with its own suet and offal, which has been thickened with oatmeal, and boiled in water or baked in the ashes of a fire.

definitions.definition: A type of cake or dessert cooked usually by boiling or steaming.

quote.citation: 2007, Magdaleen Van Wyk, The Complete South African Cookbook, page 265:
quote.text: Steamed puddings, a favourite for winter, are both easy to make and delicious. Served with one of the sweet sauces (recipes 497 to 506) they make a filling and satisfying end to a meal.

definitions.definition: A type of dessert that has a texture similar to custard or mousse but using some kind of starch as the thickening agent.
(UK, Australia, New Zealand) Dessert; the dessert course of a meal.
(originally) A sausage made primarily from blood.

quote.citation: 2005, Ruzbeh N. Bharucha, Rest in Pieces, page 7:
quote.text: "How is my little pudding?" Jehan nuzzles up to me and rests his little head on my shoulder, still chuckling  […]

quote.citation: 1715 November 15, To Mr James Neilsone, opposite the Tolbooth, Berwick; published as “Battle of Sheriffmuir”, in The Edinburgh Magazine, 1818 March, page 241:
quote.text: I pray God he may recover, though there is little hopes; as there is of Coll Halley, being shott throw the body; and of Capt. Urquhart of Burdyeyeards, being wounded in the belly, after being made prisoner, soe that his puddings hang out.

quote.citation: [1785, Francis Grose, A Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue‎[1]:
quote.text: PUDDINGS, the guts; I'll let out your puddings.]
Eat your pudding, slave, and hold your tongue.

definitions.definition: (archaic, slang) A piece of good fortune.
